If you’re into games where you get to build, create, and figure stuff out, Factorio is an absolute blast. You start out on an alien planet with just your wits and a few tools, but before you know it, you’re designing massive automated factories that make even your wildest LEGO creations look basic.

The graphics are simple, but honestly, that’s part of the charm—it’s all about how smart you can get with your setups. Plus, the sound of machines whirring and conveyor belts running is surprisingly satisfying.

What really makes this game epic is how much freedom you get. Want to play solo and geek out over the perfect design? Go for it.

This game is not for everyone, obviously it's a factory game, which there are very few of. The most advanced factory game on the market. Delivers hard on all fronts from graphics to game play and everything in-between.

Also the learning curve is almost completely linear. You'll start off with a small factory that produces a small amount of iron plates and quickly begin to realise how in-efficient it is and you'll tear the whole thing down and start again only the repeat this process again and again and again until you're producing as many steel plates as you possibly can whilst taking up the least space possible. you can then apply that knowledge to your other factories were the cycle will repeat itself. Eventually you'll have massive sprawling factories that make sense only to you. it's like a language only you can speak. you'll then look back at tiny in-efficient factory and realise how far you've come within only 3 hours, or so you thought as you glance at the clock and realise that you've actually been playing for over 16 hours now.

What i'm getting at is that this is game that hook you in as you optimise for hours and hours on end. if you have a life to throw away buy this game, you wont regret it.

Well, with very few words: One of the best games I've ever experienced to play.

No lie, the game industry these days s*cks *ss, especially those early access alpha and beta games which never will be more than an idea and a scribble than an actual game. However, Factorio is different, way different, it's early access, but in a state where it's better balanced and developed than most triple A games. - So, I could write a story about my experience but let's sum it up - if you like logical thought, building, surviving, developing, creating, playing around and stuff like this, spend your bucks on this title(!), you surely won't be disappointed - it's totally worth it!
I've had a hard time thinking about anything else since I've started playing this game.

Do you feel like you don't fit in into normal everyday life?
Can't scratch that feeling that something is wrong, like there's an invisible wall between you and other people?

Do you ever wonder if you are on the spectrum but don't have the neccessary help available to find out?

Well you don't have to wonder anymore, just download this game and you'll find out.

Being completely new to this type of game the learning curve might feel a bit steep, but not overwhelmingly so. Once you get the hang of automating your factory, seeing the results is extremely rewarding!
The aliens feel more like a nuisance than a real threat. However, personally I wouldn't want combat to be too big of a mechanic. I like how it's just an extra dimension next to just building stuff.

Taking what you've learned and applying that to a new factory and having the fruits of your labor actually pay off is a fantastic way to see the precious hours of a day go by more rapidly than the mental decline of a modern day feminist.

It's Factorio! The base game has some strange material requirement scaling on the last two science pack types(suddenly you need like 10x as much resources per pack), but it's still pretty good. The top modded overhauls have smoother progression, and I enjoyed them a bit more.

You don't necessarily have to make a huge base to play this game, but you sure can! I generally found it difficult to scale up a base without either doing a lot of long term planning at the start or just accepting that I would have to redo my early setups.

Factorio:
— Where Fun Meets Conveyor Belt Nightmares

Review:
I thought Factorio would be a quick, fun distraction. Now, 500+ hours later, I’m dreaming about conveyor belts, blueprinting factories in my head, and wondering why I can’t be this organized in real life.

Why It’s Awesome:

You start alone and end up turning an entire planet into your factory playground.
Watching machines work together is oddly satisfying —until one belt ruins everything.
“Just one more conveyor” is a lie. You’ll be up at 3 a.m. building the perfect setup.

Funny Realizations:

Pollution? Eh, who cares… until the biters show up, then it’s panic mode.
Conveyor spaghetti is a real thing. One wrong belt, and your factory turns into chaos.
Multiplayer is chaos. Either you’re building together like pros or screaming about why coal is in the copper line.

Little Problems:

This game makes you feel smart—right until you realize your belts go in circles.
Biters aren’t just enemies —they’re nature’s way of telling you, “You’re the problem.”

Final Thoughts:
Factorio isn’t just a game; it’s a way of life. Build, automate, and completely lose track of time. It’s fun, frustrating, and somehow, I can’t stop playing.

Rating: 9/10 – "500 hours in, and it’s still a chaotic experiment that somehow went right."

You basically play an engineer guy who crashed into a planet full of disgusting creatures and natural resources. And you are right, you are in this planet to spread democracy(Accidentally)! You leech the natural resources and use them to leech more of them. As you leech more resources, you get more influence on this planet due to your much more better technology level and production capacity.

Are you gonna stop expanding your factory and influence? Nah. You double the production capacity, you fuck up the lake with pollution that was clear as the sky when you arrived the planet. Now the creatures of the planet are angry because of the pollution, are you gonna leave the planet in peace? Nah. You launch a fucking nuclear warhead on them so they stop coming. Do they stop? Nah. Now my friend, you are in the infinite loop of Factorio and you are not going to stop enjoying it anytime soon.

Can you automate? I can, but up to a point. At some point it gets.. overwhelming, and I don't have the single-person lifestyle to take hours figuring it out. But, you might. It's fun trying to get everything to work right. If you like puzzles, you'll like this. Just remember to make bullets, and spacebar is your trigger. :)

I like to draw a lot of parallels between playing Factorio and writing code. You're given an endgoal - the point you want to reach, and left to your own devices with a set of resources. How you reach that endgoal and what it looks like are entirely up to you! The majority of the problems and challenges you need to overcome in this game are created by your own actions. A decision you made early in the game could hamper your efforts later on, forcing you to tear it down and redesign it, or to work around it, in the same way that a piece of code written early on in a project might later prove to be insufficient for the purpose, and need to be redesigned. But what happens when that piece of code (or factory) is relied upon by other parts?

You end up with a lot of load-bearing skeletons in your closet!
